events.text: Under the banners of the Will of Heaven nothing on the field is allowed a shadow. {hw_Foe} has dammed the river of prayers that feeds your wing: a whole world's evening prayers, backed up behind a wall of old oaths. Your quartermaster, a small god of granaries named Pell, says the line has two days of faith left in it.

ok.log: The wall of oaths cracks under your hands and the prayers come down in a flood. Your soldiers stand up straighter all along the line. Below, a world's evening suddenly feels heard.

fail.log: The oaths hold. They were sworn by people who meant them. You come back with your hands numb and Pell rationing the faith by the spoonful.

choices.text: Feed the line from a smaller world

effects.log: Pell finds a tiny world whose prayers nobody draws on: mostly about goats. It is enough. Your soldiers fight the next week with a strange fondness for goats.

choices.text: Ask the praying world to pray elsewhere

effects.log: You send a dream asking them to pray at dawn instead. They do, puzzled, and the dam stands empty. The foe spent a year building it.

events.text: The sun-gods ride in front, where every world below can see them. {hw_Foe} is besieging a sky-fortress on {hw_field}, and to starve it they have pulled the tides of a thousand seas against its walls. Below, fishers in a thousand worlds wake to find their boats sitting on mud.

choices.text: Break the siege before the seas are ruined

ok.log: You hit the tide-gods where they are anchored, and the seas let go with a long sigh. A thousand harbours fill again by evening. The fortress cheers.

fail.log: You hit too early. The tide-gods hold, and the fortress has to wait another month. Below, the mud starts to smell.

choices.text: Send fish to the stranded harbours

effects.log: You cannot lift the siege, but you can open a small river of fish into every dry bay. The fishers below call it the Year of Easy Fish and never learn why.

choices.text: Wait for the tides to turn on their own

effects.log: Tides are older than any pantheon. In nine days they shrug the foe off, and the siege ends by itself. Nobody gets a medal.

events.text: Fire runs along the line of the Will of Heaven like a lit fuse. A minor god of a small mountain has walked off the line. His name is Oru, his mountain is four hundred feet tall, and he says nobody up here ever learned its name. He is sitting on a rock behind your lines, eating an apple.

choices.text: Learn the name of his mountain and ask him back

ok.log: It is called Little Hat. You say it twice. Oru finishes his apple and walks back to the line, and he holds the ford all winter.

fail.log: You call it Little Cap. Oru looks at you for a long time, and leaves for home.

choices.text: Let him go home to it

effects.log: Oru goes home. Below, a village under Little Hat has its best spring in living memory. The officers mutter that you are soft.
Oru is marched back in chains of light. He holds his post, silently, and he never once looks at you again.

events.text: Under the banners of the Will of Heaven nothing on the field is allowed a shadow. {hw_cmdr} rides out alone onto {hw_field} and asks for you. The worlds below will see this duel as an eclipse, a very long one. {hw_friend} grips your arm. "You do not have to. Nobody down there will know which shadow was yours."

ok.log: You fight until the eclipse has lasted three days below. {hw_cmdr} yields with a nod that costs them something. Your side roars.

fail.log: You are thrown, hard. {hw_cmdr} lets you limp back to your lines without a word. The eclipse ends early.

effects.log: {hw_friend} rides out, grinning, and fights {hw_cmdr} to a draw. The eclipse below is a short one. {hw_friend} talks about it for a year.
You send word that you have a war to run. {hw_cmdr} rides back and the eclipse becomes a cloudy afternoon. Some call you wise, some other things.

events.text: The sun-gods ride in front, where every world below can see them. Your wing is ordered to throw a comet at {hw_foe}'s left flank. The comet has a name, Old Tasso, and has been circling quietly for nine thousand years. Its keeper, a dusty god of almanacs named Brin, begs you to pick another one.

effects.log: Old Tasso goes in like the end of an argument and the flank breaks. Brin crosses out a line in nine thousand almanacs and does not speak to you again.
You find a young comet with no name and no fans. It does half the job. Brin sends you a calendar every year after that.

choices.text: Throw a cloud of old calendars instead

effects.log: Brin's own idea. A blizzard of paper days falls on the flank and nobody over there knows what date it is for a week. It works better than it should.

events.text: Fire runs along the line of the Will of Heaven like a lit fuse. An order reaches you: burn the dreams of the world {hw_world} so the foe cannot hide scouts in them. Four billion people would wake up blank for a year. The seal on the order is real. The handwriting shakes.

effects.log: You refuse it, and sign your name. There is an inquiry. In the end the order is quietly withdrawn, and so is your next promotion.

choices.text: Burn only the dreams near the border

effects.log: You burn a strip of dreams along the coast. A few million people sleep badly and grey for a season. It is a smaller wrong, and you carry it anyway.

choices.text: Find the scouts in the dreams instead

ok.log: You walk the dreams yourself for a week and pull out eleven foe scouts by the collar. The dreamers only remember a stranger who apologised.

fail.log: The scouts hide better than you seek. You come back with dream-dust in your hair and nothing to show the officer who sent the order.

events.text: Under the banners of the Will of Heaven nothing on the field is allowed a shadow. Your banner-bearer is the god of one lighthouse on one rocky coast, a quiet youngster named Fen, who volunteered because nobody ever looks at a lighthouse by day. Halfway across {hw_field}, the banner pole snaps.

choices.text: Give Fen your own spear for a pole

effects.log: Fen holds the banner up on your spear and does not lower it all day. The whole wing follows a lighthouse home. You fight with a borrowed stick.
Fen drops the cloth and lights up. A lighthouse in full beam turns out to be a very good banner. The foe's archers cannot look at it.

choices.text: Order the line to hold without a banner

effects.log: The line holds, uneasy. Fen spends the evening mending the pole and apologising to it.

events.text: The sun-gods ride in front, where every world below can see them. The foe opens with hail the size of small moons. Most of it misses. One piece is coming down on the field hospital, where a goddess of minor fevers named Aunt Meru is sewing up a river-god who will not stop talking.

ok.log: You catch a moon of ice on your shoulders and set it down outside the tent. Aunt Meru does not look up. "Thank you, dear. Shut the flap."

fail.log: You turn it aside but not enough: it takes the supply tent. The river-god finally stops talking.

choices.text: Melt it with a prayer of summer

effects.log: It comes down as a warm and very heavy rain. The hospital floods to the ankles. Aunt Meru has opinions about that.
You move it in time, river-god and all. He talks about it for a century.

You take the far end in one rush. The rainbow comes back missing indigo. In a thousand worlds below, painters cannot find the right blue for a generation.

effects.log: Three days lost, nobody seen. Iridi waves from her bridge as you pass far below it.

events.text: The Green Assembly fights the way roots fight a stone: patiently, and from below. The only way across {hw_field} is a rainbow, and the foe watches its far end. Its goddess, Iridi, will hold it for one crossing. First she would like to know whether you mean to bring it back in one piece.

effects.log: You cross at a walk, single file, nobody stamping. Iridi gets her rainbow back with one colour a little scuffed. She forgives you the scuff.
You take the far end in one rush. The rainbow comes back missing indigo. In a thousand worlds below, painters cannot find the right blue for a generation.

events.text: Under the banners of the Will of Heaven nothing on the field is allowed a shadow. Your scouts bring in a prisoner: the goddess of a single well in a desert world. She swore to {hw_foe} because they were the only ones who ever answered her. Her world has been dry since she left it.

effects.log: She goes back to her well on her word. The desert world below gets its water back. {hw_Foe} never gets her back.
She knows where {hw_foe} draws its water. It is a small piece of news, and it wins a small battle. She asks every morning when she can go home.

choices.text: Keep her, and send the well a cup a day yourself

effects.log: You pour a cup of rain down her well each dawn. It is not enough for a world, but it is enough for a village. She notices.

ok.log: Each soldier prays a little when they are lost. You follow the sound and turn the wing a quarter. The mountain-god sleeps on.

effects.log: The whole field hears it, foe included. Your wing comes home. So does half of theirs, by mistake, and surrenders out of embarrassment.

events.text: Under the banners of the Will of Heaven nothing on the field is allowed a shadow. A constellation of the Great Bear has broken loose in the fighting, seven stars of panicking bear, and it is coming down {hw_field} towards both lines at once.

choices.text: Open your ranks and let it through

effects.log: The bear thunders through your gap and into the foe's line, which did not think of that. Everyone counts it as yours.

ok.log: You walk up with your hands open, and it lies down at your feet like a large starry dog. Both armies watch. Nobody fights that afternoon.

fail.log: It does not care for your hands. You spend the afternoon up a sky-tree.

effects.log: The line holds and the bear goes round. A shield-god named Tamsa gets a bruise the shape of the Plough.

events.text: The sun-gods ride in front, where every world below can see them. Your forge is out of thunderbolts. Haru, the smith-god who makes them, has a sprained wrist and a temper. "I could make you lightning," Haru says, "but it will be the cheap sort. It forks."

effects.log: It forks. Some of it hits the foe, some hits a hill, one fork hits your own baggage. The battle is won, roughly.

choices.text: Bind Haru's wrist and wait a day

effects.log: You bind it yourself. Haru makes nine perfect bolts the next morning, grumbling, and names one after you.
You fight a day with spears and stubbornness. You hold your ground, no more.

events.text: Fire runs along the line of the Will of Heaven like a lit fuse. Soldiers of {hw_foe} wave a pale cloud on a pole: they want to carry their wounded off {hw_field}. Your archers are ready. One of them, a hunting-god named Kesh, says it could be a trick.

effects.log: They carry off forty gods, slowly, and one of them salutes you at the edge of the field. It was not a trick.
You let them, with every bow drawn. Nobody does anything foolish. Both sides go home a little more tired.
The cloud is lowered. The wounded are carried off that night anyway, under fire. You hear them for a long time.

events.text: Under the banners of the Will of Heaven nothing on the field is allowed a shadow. An old watchtower on {hw_field} is held by a retired god of sentries, Grandfather Lusk, who has kept it through four wars and will not leave for this one. The foe will be here by noon.

effects.log: You hold it till dusk with Lusk shouting directions. He knows every loose stone. The foe goes round, eventually.
You carry him out over your shoulder while he kicks. The tower falls an hour later. He does not thank you, but he lives in your camp and corrects your sentries.
He holds it alone till noon and then, somehow, past noon. When you come back the tower is still standing and Lusk is asleep in it.

events.text: The sun-gods ride in front, where every world below can see them. The foe has raised a wave the height of a mountain to throw at your line. It has to cross a small world called Pemmery on the way, and nobody in Pemmery has ever heard of either pantheon.

choices.text: Turn the wave before it reaches Pemmery

ok.log: You meet it at sea and turn it aside with your shoulder. It breaks on an empty ocean. Pemmery has a very high tide and a festival.

fail.log: You only slow it. Pemmery's harbour is flooded to the chimneys. Nobody is lost, but nobody is pleased.

choices.text: Warn Pemmery in a dream and let the wave come on

effects.log: Pemmery goes up into its hills overnight. The wave washes their empty town and then hits your line, much tired. You hold.

choices.text: Let it hit Pemmery and then your line

effects.log: It spends itself on Pemmery. Your line is dry. Somebody in the camp calls it efficient. You do not answer them.

events.text: Under the banners of the Will of Heaven nothing on the field is allowed a shadow. Your mount is a horse made of a small constellation, old and steady, named Pilgrim. In the middle of the charge Pilgrim stops dead and will not go on. There is no reason you can see.

effects.log: You wait. A second later the ground ahead opens into a pit of old night. The charge goes round it. You give Pilgrim extra stars that evening.
You run on alone and find the pit by falling into it. Pilgrim pulls you out by the collar.
Pilgrim goes on, ears flat, and you both go into the pit. It takes a day to climb out.

You run on alone and find the pit by falling into it. Pilgrim pulls you out by the collar.
Pilgrim goes on, ears flat, and you both go into the pit. It takes a day to climb out.

events.text: The sun-gods ride in front, where every world below can see them. A trickster of {hw_foe} has stolen your voice, and is shouting orders with it all over {hw_field}. Your soldiers are retreating in three directions at once.

effects.log: You wave flags for the rest of the day, like a ship. It works. The trickster gets bored and gives your voice back with a cough in it.

ok.log: You catch them by the ear, and your voice comes out of their mouth saying sorry.

fail.log: They lead you round the field twice. Your voice comes back the next day, hoarse.

events.text: Fire runs along the line of the Will of Heaven like a lit fuse. You wake to find {hw_foe} has planted a forest in the middle of your line overnight. It is a lovely forest. It has owls. Half your wing is lost in it.

effects.log: The owls know exactly where everyone is and are very smug about it. By noon your wing is out and the owls are on your side.
You clear a road through it, and feel bad about every tree. The wing comes out. The road stays for a thousand years.
It is a strange battle among the trunks, with a lot of apologising. Neither side gains anything except some pine needles.

events.text: Under the banners of the Will of Heaven nothing on the field is allowed a shadow. The battle is set for the third hour. The god of that hour, a small anxious being called Tertia, has come to ask if it could be moved to the fourth. She has never had a battle in her and she is worried she will be remembered for it.

choices.text: Move it to the fourth hour

effects.log: The fourth hour, a big cheerful god, is delighted. The battle goes well. Tertia brings you tea at the third hour every day after.

choices.text: Fight at the third, and tell her it will be remembered well

effects.log: You fight well, partly for her. In the worlds below, the third hour is a lucky one for a thousand years.
You fight at the third. Tertia watches from a corner, wringing her hands, and every clock below runs slow.

events.text: The sun-gods ride in front, where every world below can see them. {hw_Foe} has pulled a whole inhabited world in front of their line as a shield. It is a gentle little world of rice and kites. Every shot you take at them has to go through it.

effects.log: You hold fire. The foe sits behind their world, smug, until the world's own god turns up and shouts at them. They let it go by evening.

ok.log: You take the long way and hit them from behind their shield. They had not thought of a behind.

fail.log: The long way is longer than the map said. You lose a day and some feeling in your feet.

effects.log: The world's god, a mild kite-maker called Linnet, rows up personally and takes it back. {hw_Foe} cannot argue with a god in her own sky.

effects.log: You hold the ford together until the last cart is over. You both come home soaked and pleased with yourselves.

You bring the bank down. Nobody crosses after you, and nobody crosses there for an age. The farmers below lose their road.

events.text: The camp of the Will of Heaven is never dark, and nobody in it has slept properly in years. The prayers that come up to your tent each night are sorted by a tired clerk-god called Abbo. Tonight he hands you one from a child in {hw_world}: please bring back my cat from the war. The cat is, it seems, a cat-god, and in your wing.

choices.text: Find the cat-god and send him home on leave

effects.log: He goes, tail up. Below, a child finds a cat on the step. Abbo says he will never get the paperwork right again.

choices.text: Write the child a dream instead

effects.log: You send a dream of the cat being brave. It is true, and it helps. The cat stays and catches the foe's message-mice all winter.

events.text: In the sun-camp the tents glow from inside, and the cooks complain about it. The camp cook is the god of exactly one dish, porridge, and he is very good at it. The soldiers have eaten porridge for nine years. A deputation asks you, in the nicest possible way, to do something.

effects.log: You borrow a goddess of soups from a neighbouring wing. The porridge-god sulks for a week, then they start cooking together, and morale leaps.
You eat it publicly, twice, with relish. The cook weeps. The deputation goes away defeated and slightly fond of you.

choices.text: Ask the cook for porridge with things in it

effects.log: He has never thought of things in it. The next morning there is honey. It is a revolution.

events.text: The Will of Heaven keeps its camp on a hill, so it can be seen from everywhere. A river-god of your wing, Old Tanno, took a wound across his middle, and below, in a world called Haddow, his river is running slow and brown. Farms all along it are watching the water.

choices.text: Sit up with him and tend it

effects.log: You change the dressing every hour. By the third night the river below runs clear. Haddow has a good year and never knows why.

choices.text: Send him home to heal in his own bed

effects.log: He goes home to his springs and heals in a month. You are one god short at the ford.

choices.text: Ask the healers to hurry him

effects.log: They hurry. He fights again in a week, and the river below has floods all summer.

events.text: The camp of the Will of Heaven is never dark, and nobody in it has slept properly in years. The offerings ledger does not add up. A world's harvest festival should have sent up eight hundred loaves of praise. The wing got six hundred. The quartermaster, a sleek god of storehouses called Varro, says the rest was spoiled in transit.

ok.log: Varro has been selling praise to a rival wing. You make him pay it all back, loaf by loaf, and put him on porridge.

fail.log: His books are too good. You find nothing, and he knows you looked.

choices.text: Let it go and watch him

effects.log: You let it go. The next festival's offerings arrive in full. Varro has noticed you noticing.

choices.text: Make him walk the supply line himself

effects.log: Varro walks the river of prayers end to end. He comes back thin, honest and badly sunburnt.

events.text: In the sun-camp the tents glow from inside, and the cooks complain about it. Around the fire the soldiers are singing a hymn from a world below, a very old one, very badly. They are singing it to you. You realise it is about you, and that the world which wrote it got almost every detail wrong.

effects.log: You sing the wrong verses with them, loudly. The soldiers talk about it for a decade.
You correct them, gently. They sing it right the next night, and it is somehow much less good.
You listen from the dark. In the morning you feel better about the war than you have in a year.

events.text: The Will of Heaven keeps its camp on a hill, so it can be seen from everywhere. A new recruit, a shy god of thresholds named Dorran, gets all his prayers from worlds that worship {hw_foe}. {hw_friend} thinks he is a spy. Dorran says doors are doors, whoever opens them.

effects.log: You give him the gate watch. He keeps it for three years and lets nobody through who should not come. Doors are doors.

ok.log: You leave a false plan where he can see it. It goes nowhere. He is not a spy, and he never learns you checked.

fail.log: He finds the false plan, reads it, and hands it back to you, hurt. You apologise.

effects.log: Dorran goes to the rear and guards a cupboard. The cupboard is never once opened by anyone who should not.

effects.log: You judge, which is worse. Everyone disagrees with you. It is the best night the camp has had all year.

events.text: In the sun-camp the tents glow from inside, and the cooks complain about it. Your armour was forged out of a particular dawn, the first of the war, and it needs polishing with a soft cloth and a little hope every morning. Your squire, a young god of buttons named Pim, has run out of hope.

choices.text: Polish it yourself and talk to Pim

effects.log: You polish it together. Pim finds some hope in the talking, and the armour shines pink.
You go out in a grey dawn. Nobody can see you on the field, which is useful, and sad.

choices.text: Send Pim home for a month

effects.log: Pim goes home to the worlds of buttons and comes back full of hope and with new buttons for everyone.

events.text: The Will of Heaven keeps its camp on a hill, so it can be seen from everywhere. A minor god of your wing has faded: the god of a mountain pass that nobody uses since the road was built below. His name was Aster. His world has already forgotten him. Somebody has to speak at the fire.

effects.log: You speak, and you find you know more about Aster than you thought. The soldiers stand. Below, for one night, a few travellers take the old pass.

choices.text: Find the last traveller who prayed to him and bring them up in a dream

effects.log: An old shepherd comes up in her sleep and says she always liked that pass. It is the shortest and best funeral the camp has seen.

choices.text: Take him on as a runner

effects.log: He runs messages all through the rain season and never once gets them wet. The soldiers adore him.
You send him to the rear with a letter. He sends back one complaint a day for a year.
He opens up over the mess tent, and for the first time in years supper is dry.

events.text: In the sun-camp the tents glow from inside, and the cooks complain about it. The whole camp says the war will end by the solstice. Nobody knows where it started. {hw_friend} has already packed. You know it will not end by the solstice.

effects.log: They take it hard, but they take it. Nobody deserts at the solstice, because nobody was waiting for it.
The solstice comes and goes. There is a bad week after. Then they hope for the next one.
You throw a feast at the solstice as if it were the end. It is not, but it is a very good feast.

events.text: The Will of Heaven keeps its camp on a hill, so it can be seen from everywhere. One of the hounds of the great hunt has strayed into camp, an enormous grey creature called Patience who has decided she is now yours. She eats as much as a squadron. The hunt-god wants her back.

effects.log: Patience goes back to the hunt, looking over her shoulder. The hunt-god owes you a favour and pays it at the next battle.

choices.text: Ask the hunt-god to let her stay

effects.log: He sighs and lets her. Patience guards your tent for the rest of the war and nobody ever steals your boots.
You let her stand between you. She sits on the hunt-god's foot, looking at you. It is decided by evening, and the foot is fine.

events.text: The camp of the Will of Heaven is never dark, and nobody in it has slept properly in years. The oldest soldier in camp is a goddess of shields called Marrow who has fought in three wars in heaven and says this one is the stupidest yet. She says it in front of the officers, often.

choices.text: Tell her to keep it down

effects.log: She keeps it down. She also stops telling you where the foe will come from, which she was always right about.
She is appalled, and then excellent at it. The officers complain about her for years.

effects.log: Everyone tightens their belts. The wing is lean and short-tempered and holds.

events.text: The Will of Heaven keeps its camp on a hill, so it can be seen from everywhere. A note on your camp table, in a careful hand: I have gone home to my bees. I am sorry. They do not understand war and neither do I. Thessaly, goddess of the hives of one valley.

effects.log: You strike her from the roll as on leave. Her valley has honey in a bad year. The officers say nothing, pointedly.
{hw_friend} brings her back, with bees. The bees are now in the camp. They are, it turns out, quite good at war.
You find her in her valley among the hives and you stay to help with the honey for a day. She comes back with you of her own will.

effects.log: Peace in the mess. Below, the delta dries in one half and floods in the other.

ok.log: You draw them a fair line. They accept it, sulking, and it holds a thousand years.

fail.log: They both hate your line, and for once agree on something.

You write it all. A country below has a long, honest autumn. It rains, and the crops are fine.
No weather at all goes down. A country has a strange flat week. Somebody at home worries.

events.text: In the sun-camp the tents glow from inside, and the cooks complain about it. Two of your officers are quarrelling over whose world was hit hardest in the last battle. One lost a forest, the other a lake. Both are right, and it is beginning to spread through the camp.

effects.log: The camp goes hungry for two days. Below, a forest and a lake are healing. The quarrel stops.
It stops, on the surface. Under it, both officers stop speaking to you as well.
You take them down to see each other's worlds. They come back quiet and friendly.

Below, a world called Calloway is holding its great festival, the one to the god in your wing who owns its harvest, a round red goddess called Mab. She wants to go and be there. It is the night before a battle.

choices.text: Let her go for the night

effects.log: Mab goes and comes back before dawn, glowing, full of the festival. She fights like three gods in the morning.
She stays. Calloway has its festival and its harvest anyway, but a little quieter. Mab fights well and says nothing.

choices.text: Bring the festival up to the camp

effects.log: You ask Calloway, in a dream, to light a few extra lanterns. They float all the way up to the camp. The whole wing celebrates.

events.text: In the sun-camp the tents glow from inside, and the cooks complain about it. The wing's best messenger mount, a horse of falling stars called Comet's Daughter, has gone lame in the near fore. The farrier-god says it is a stone of old night in the hoof, very deep.

effects.log: She rests. The wing's messages go slower all season and two orders arrive late.

events.text: The lesser gods of the Will of Heaven read the war news on the sky, like everyone else. Three gods have turned up at your door whose worlds were swallowed in the fighting on {hw_field}: a goddess of a lake, a god of a market town, a very small god of a well-loved bench. They have no domains left and nowhere to sit.

choices.text: Give them corners of your own domain

effects.log: The lake-goddess takes a pond, the market-god a crossroads, the bench-god a bench. Your domain is more crowded and more loved.

choices.text: Find them work at the front

effects.log: They go to the war, having nothing else. The bench-god turns out to be excellent at holding a position.

choices.text: Write to the Book of Fates for them

effects.log: The clerks promise to look into it, in an age or two. The three stay with you meanwhile and fill your hall with complaints.

events.text: In the bright halls of the Will of Heaven the war arrives as smoke on the horizon. A priest in a world below, an earnest young man named Odel, has been praying for nine days to ask why the sun rises late. The honest answer is that the sun-god of his world is at the front and the deputy keeps oversleeping.

choices.text: Tell him the truth in a dream

effects.log: Odel wakes and preaches a sermon on patience that is the best of his life. His congregation sets their clocks back.

choices.text: Go and wake the deputy yourself

effects.log: The deputy, a large drowsy god called Morrow, gets up on time for a month out of shame. Odel thanks the heavens.
The sun goes on rising late. Odel's world invents a new hour to put the gap in. It becomes a very popular hour for naps.

events.text: Far from the front, the sun-halls still cast no shadows, but they cast a great deal of worry. The war has made prayers dear. In the markets of heaven a single heartfelt prayer for rain now costs what a whole festival cost before the war. Lesser gods are going hungry, and a price-god named Fennick is buying up the rest.

choices.text: Share your own offerings with the lesser gods

effects.log: You open your storehouse. It lasts a season. Fennick is furious, which is a good sign.

choices.text: Shame Fennick in the market square

ok.log: He sells at a fair price by evening, sweating. The lesser gods eat.

fail.log: He shrugs, and raises his prices to spite you.

choices.text: Buy a stock while you still can

effects.log: You buy a cellar of prayers. They keep. You feel worse about them than you expected.

events.text: The lesser gods of the Will of Heaven read the war news on the sky, like everyone else. The town crier of heaven, a large and very loud goddess named Bellow, has started reading out the losses as well as the victories. The lesser gods are frightened, and the high gods want her silenced.

choices.text: Defend her right to read them

effects.log: She keeps reading. People are frightened, and they are also prepared. Bellow sends you a gift of a small, quiet bell.

choices.text: Ask her to read them more gently

effects.log: She tries. Bellow being gentle is still very loud, but kinder.
She is silenced by the end of the month. The rumours that replace her are much worse.

events.text: In the bright halls of the Will of Heaven the war arrives as smoke on the horizon. The school where young gods learn to answer prayers has closed: all its teachers are at the front. Thirty small gods are running loose in heaven, answering prayers wrong. A world has had snow in summer.

choices.text: Teach them yourself for a season

effects.log: You teach thirty small gods how to answer a prayer. It is the hardest season of the war, and the best.
You coax a very old god of slates and chalk out of retirement. He is strict. The snow stops.

choices.text: Give each of them one prayer

effects.log: Each small god gets one prayer to answer, and only one. They do it with great seriousness.

events.text: Far from the front, the sun-halls still cast no shadows, but they cast a great deal of worry. A world below has lost its god in the war. Its people still pray every evening to an empty sky. The prayers drift up and pile against the gate of heaven like leaves. Nobody is assigned to them.

choices.text: Answer them yourself for a while

effects.log: You answer that world's prayers in your evenings, small things mostly. It is exhausting. The people below say their god has come back changed.
You find a young goddess who wants a world. She is clumsy and devoted. The world forgives her both.

choices.text: Leave the prayers at the gate

effects.log: The leaves pile up. In a hundred years the world below stops praying and becomes a very practical place.

events.text: The lesser gods of the Will of Heaven read the war news on the sky, like everyone else. A hymn written by {hw_foe}'s worlds has been banned in heaven for the war. It is a very beautiful hymn. Everyone hums it anyway. A censor-god named Pruett has asked you to report the hummers.

choices.text: Hum it in front of him

effects.log: Pruett writes down your name. It becomes a small scandal. The hymn becomes more popular.

choices.text: Report a few, to keep the peace

effects.log: A few lesser gods are fined. The humming goes quieter, and colder.
He looks at you for a long time and then crosses your name off his list. You hum it later, in private.

events.text: In the bright halls of the Will of Heaven the war arrives as smoke on the horizon. A summons has come for an old friend of yours, a sleepy god of a quiet bay named Hollin, who has not fought in an age. He is not suited to war. He has packed anyway, and forgotten his boots.

choices.text: Bring him his boots and see him off

effects.log: You bring the boots. He goes. He writes every week, terrible letters, full of complaints about the food.
You call in a favour. Hollin guards a quiet bay at the edge of the war, which suits him, and nobody ever gets past it.
You take his summons. Hollin goes back to sleep in his bay, grateful and guilty.

events.text: Far from the front, the sun-halls still cast no shadows, but they cast a great deal of worry. The lesser gods of your domain are planting gardens for the front: rows of small prayers, quick to grow, that ripen into courage. A goat-god keeps eating the courage.

effects.log: You fence it. The goat-god eats the fence, then the courage. You give up and plant more.
You make him watchman over the garden. He eats only the weeds now, and is proud of it.
He becomes very brave. He goes to the front himself and turns out to be a terror.

events.text: The lesser gods of the Will of Heaven read the war news on the sky, like everyone else. Gods are coming home from the front, and some come home with their domains changed. A goddess of a summer river has come home cold. The river below her now freezes in August.

effects.log: You sit with her in silence on her banks for a week. Slowly, the river warms a degree.

choices.text: Find a fire-god to visit her

effects.log: A cheerful fire-god visits her daily. By autumn the river is merely cool. They talk of a joint domain.
She is left alone with the cold. The people below learn to skate in August.

events.text: Far from the front, the sun-halls still cast no shadows, but they cast a great deal of worry. The old goddess next door, Granny Fleece, has been knitting clouds for the soldiers' bedding since the war began. Her eyes are going. She has asked you to thread her needle, and then the next nine needles.

effects.log: You stay the evening, threading. She talks about the last war, and the one before. You learn a great deal about clouds.

choices.text: Find her a pair of spectacles

effects.log: You have a pair made of clear sky. She knits faster than ever, and better, and complains about the frame.

choices.text: Pour a little water down every night

choices.text: Petition for her to be sent home

effects.log: In a year she is sent home. The fisherfolk pray in thanks, mostly to her, a little to you.
You send a dream. They wait on the flats, patient. She does return, after the war.

events.text: The weather over your domain has turned to argument: the Throne of Storms wants an answer. With the summons comes a gift: a river of offerings, already turned to flow into your domain. It will keep your lesser gods fed for a century. It will stop if you say no.

choices.text: Accept the river and the war

effects.log: The river flows. Your lesser gods eat well. You march when you are called.
You dam it with your own hands and turn it home. The pantheon is offended and impressed in about equal parts.

choices.text: Keep the river and refuse the war

effects.log: You keep it a year before it is quietly turned away. Nobody up here forgets a thing like that.

events.text: A herald of the Will of Heaven arrives at noon, because they always arrive at noon. It is not only the pantheon asking. A world below that prays to you has been praying, for a year, that you will not go to war. A schoolteacher there, Abel Norrey, writes his prayer out fresh each night.

effects.log: You send Norrey a quiet summer. He takes it as an answer. The pantheon takes it as an insult.

choices.text: Go, and send Norrey a dream to explain

effects.log: He wakes and writes the dream down. He stops praying against it, and starts praying for you.

choices.text: Go, and say nothing to him

effects.log: Norrey's prayers go on, every night, all through the war. You read every one.

events.text: The sky over your domain turns a hard, approving gold: the Will of Heaven is asking. The summons reminds you, politely, that this pantheon once lent you a whole spring, long ago, when your domain was dying of a drought. It does not say you owe them. It does not need to.

effects.log: You go to war on an old spring. It feels right and very heavy.

choices.text: Offer to pay it some other way

effects.log: You offer a hundred springs instead. They take the springs, sourly, and leave you be.

choices.text: Argue the debt was paid long ago

ok.log: You find the old receipt, written in rain. It was paid. They withdraw, with a grudging bow.

fail.log: You cannot find the receipt. Everyone now thinks you are both ungrateful and disorganised.

events.text: A herald of the Will of Heaven arrives at noon, because they always arrive at noon. There is a place in heaven where the neutral gods sit out every war: a long shady hall of gods of clocks, ink, salt and string. A god of string named Tobin has saved you a seat.

effects.log: You sit out the war among the neutrals. It is peaceful and very dull. You learn a great deal about string.
You thank Tobin and go to war. He keeps the seat, just in case.

choices.text: Sit there a while to think

effects.log: You sit among the neutrals for a season. Tobin never once asks what you will do.

events.text: The sky over your domain turns a hard, approving gold: the Will of Heaven is asking. The summons is carried by a seer who says there is a prophecy, a very old one, that names you in this war. She will not tell you which side wins. She says, with great kindness, that you will be remembered either way.

choices.text: Take your place in the prophecy

effects.log: You join. The seer nods as if a kettle has boiled. You wonder for the rest of the war what she knows.

choices.text: Refuse to be in a prophecy

effects.log: You refuse. The seer writes something on her sleeve and goes away. You will never know if that was in it too.

choices.text: Ask her to read your own fate instead

ok.log: She reads a long and quiet life with one great kindness in it. It is enough to decide you, either way.

fail.log: She reads, frowns, and declines to say. You sleep badly for a year.

effects.log: You stand in his valley all through the war, not on anybody's side. Nobody tramples it.

events.text: The sky over your domain turns a hard, approving gold: the Will of Heaven is asking. The summons has terms. A good command, a fair share of any domain taken, and a promise that your own worlds will not be asked to send their prayers to the front. It is an honest offer. It is still a war.

effects.log: You sign. The terms are kept, to the letter, and the war takes everything the letter does not cover.
You ask for your worlds to be kept out of the fighting entirely. To your surprise they agree, and you go.
You decline politely. The terms are offered to somebody else, who takes them.

Since the summons came you have dreamt of the war every night: long lines of gods in the sky, worlds below turning their faces up. choices.text: Ask a dream-god what it means

effects.log: The dream-god says it means you have eaten cheese late. Then, softly, that it means whatever you decide.

effects.log: You wait. The foe moves first. The chance is gone.

ok.log: You go over the cloud walls in one rush. Barrow yields to you personally, with the keys, which surprises everyone including Barrow.

fail.log: The walls hold. Barrow waves from them, cheerfully, and your wing sits down to besiege.

effects.log: You talk for a day across the wall. He agrees to leave if his soldiers can leave with him. They walk out singing.
You sit down around it. It is a long siege and Barrow is very patient.

effects.log: You promise. Now you have to keep it. You do, at a cost, every day of the war.

effects.log: You lift the river town on your shoulder and carry it back over the line. It is a heavy town.

events.text: Somewhere below, a world has gone a whole month without a sunrise, and everyone knows why. The foe has pulled the tides of a thousand seas away from your side's worlds. The seas below are drawing back from their shores. On one world, a whole village is walking out across the sea floor, looking for the water.

choices.text: Pull the tides back for one night

ok.log: You pull. The sea comes back, gently, and the village walks home ahead of it. It costs you more than you can say.

fail.log: You cannot hold it. The sea comes back too fast. The village gets out, wet, and very frightened.

choices.text: Warn the village in a dream

effects.log: They come back to shore before the tide returns. They are safe. The sea is still gone.

choices.text: Ask a child there what they would pray, if they could pray anything

effects.log: The child asks for a dog. Your hosts look at each other. A dog arrives in that world the next spring, then rather a lot of them.

events.text: You climb to the halls of the Will of Heaven, where the floors are warm underfoot. The pantheon's eldest god receives you lying down: a wound from the last war has never closed, and below, a whole world has been in autumn for nine hundred years. She would like your opinion as an outsider.

ok.log: You see a splinter of an old oath still in it. It comes out. The world below has its first spring in nine hundred years.

fail.log: You see nothing they have not seen. She thanks you for looking, which most do not.

effects.log: You sit with her through an evening. She tells you about the world in autumn. She says she has grown fond of it.

events.text: Your herald Brannoch, a god of trumpets whose voice cracks glass in nine worlds, wants to read your declaration of war in thunder across every sky. Sorrel, the goddess of the river the war is about, has come up from her banks to ask that it be read to her first. "It is my river," she says. "I would like to hear what you are saying about it."

effects.log: You read it to her by the water. She listens without a word. Then Brannoch reads it in thunder, and the worlds below shake, and Sorrel is already gone.
The declaration rolls across a thousand skies. Brannoch is radiant. Sorrel goes back to her river without having heard it from you.

events.text: The first winter of the war. {hw_Foe} holds the upper reach of Sorrel's river, you the lower. Brannoch wants to dam it so their half runs dry. Sorrel says nothing, but below, the river has started running backwards at night, which rivers do not do.

effects.log: The upper reach runs dry, and so do forty worlds that drink from it. {hw_Foe} pulls back. Sorrel's river stops running backwards, and stops running at all.
Brannoch calls it weakness in every camp. The river runs forwards again by spring.

ok.log: You take it in one winter march. The whole river is yours, and the war is suddenly half won.

fail.log: The march fails in the snow. You come back lighter by a dozen gods.

events.text: A prayer reaches you from Ysolde, a priestess in a world on the river's lower bank. Her people have had no rain for two years: the river's weather is spent on your war. She does not ask you to stop. She asks you to tell her how long. Brannoch, reading over your shoulder, says the answer is: until we win.

choices.text: Tell her the truth, and look for an end

fail.log: You cross and are thrown back. The promise breaks. Ysolde does not pray to you again.

events.text: At midnight a god of {hw_foe} walks across {hw_field} with his hands up: Corvin, a god of crossroads, with three small crossroads in his coat pockets. His worlds are starving, he says, and his side will not feed them. Your officer Hale, a grey god of watchtowers, says a god who changes sides once will do it twice.

effects.log: You take him in, and send food to his crossroads worlds. Hale sets a guard on his tent and checks it himself.

choices.text: Take him in under guard, and question him

effects.log: He tells you everything about {hw_foe}'s supply roads, which are his roads. It is very useful. He looks ashamed while he says it.

events.text: Hale brings you a letter he took from Corvin's tent. It is addressed to Wren, Corvin's sister, who still serves {hw_foe}. Hale has not opened it. "I wanted you to see I did not," he says. "Now you open it."

choices.text: Give it back to Corvin unopened

effects.log: You give it back. Corvin reads your face, nods, and sends it on. Hale says nothing. He is not pleased, and he respects it.
It is about their mother's garden, and whether the beans came up. You reseal it. Corvin knows, somehow, by morning.

events.text: Wren comes to the lines under a pale cloud of parley, alone. She is a goddess of signposts, small and fierce, and she wants her brother home. "His worlds are fed now," she says. "Because of you. That was the reason. There is no reason any more." Corvin looks at you. Hale looks at you. It is, apparently, your decision.

choices.text: Tell Corvin it is his choice

effects.log: Corvin is silent a long time. "Tell me what you would do," he says. You will not. He asks Wren for one more year, and she agrees.
You ask. He stays. Wren goes back alone, and she does not look round.

events.text: A year on. Corvin has made his choice: he is going home to {hw_foe}, to Wren and the bean garden. He comes to say goodbye with a small crossroads in his hand, a new one, the crossroads of the road between your camp and his sister's. "Somebody will need it," he says. Hale, to everybody's surprise, shakes his hand.

effects.log: You keep it on your table. After the war it becomes a real road, and Corvin and Wren come down it every solstice.

choices.text: Give him a pass through your lines forever

effects.log: You write the pass yourself. He never uses it in war. He uses it every peace.

events.text: Corvin stayed because you asked. In the next battle he is posted on the road against his sister's wing, and Wren is leading it. Hale offers to swap posts with him. Corvin says he will hold the road. He does not say against whom.

choices.text: Swap them, and take Corvin off the road

effects.log: Hale holds the road. Corvin and Wren never meet in battle. After the war they meet in their mother's garden, and Corvin brings you beans.
He holds it. Wren's wing does not come down it: she turns aside, and so does he. Both sides call it luck. It is not.

events.text: You have called the peace talks, and the first problem is the seating. At a table of gods each seat is a continent: put Ondine, {hw_foe}'s envoy, a sea-goddess whose islands were drowned in the war, too close to the window and a thousand coasts below will flood. Castor, an old judge of the Book of Fates, has brought a ruler and wants every seat exactly equal.

effects.log: Castor measures all afternoon. Every seat is equal to a hair. Ondine sits where she is put and says, coldly, that she has never been so fairly treated.

choices.text: Ask Ondine where she would like to sit

effects.log: She chooses the seat by the window, then moves it, deliberately, an inch away. The coasts below stay dry. She has made her point.

events.text: On the ninth day Ondine walks out. Her islands are not in the draft: both sides wrote round them. Your young clerk Tamsin, a goddess of footnotes who has been very quiet, comes to you with a sheaf. She has found every one of the drowned islands in the old records, one hundred and four, with their names.

choices.text: Take Tamsin's list to Ondine yourself

effects.log: You read Ondine the names on her own shore. She listens to all hundred and four, and comes back to the table.

choices.text: Put the list into the treaty and send it to her

effects.log: The list goes in as a clause. Ondine reads it in her hall and comes back the next day, without a word.

events.text: Castor has found a flaw. The treaty gives back Ondine's islands, but the tides that drowned them were your side's, and the treaty does not say who must pull them off. It will take a century of somebody's strength. If you raise it, the talks may break. If you do not, the islands come back on paper only.

choices.text: Raise it, and offer your own strength

effects.log: You say it out loud and say you will do it yourself. There is a long silence. Then {hw_foe} offers to share the weight.
Nobody notices. Tamsin notices, and looks at her hands. The treaty is ready.

events.text: The tides are being pulled back, a mile a year, by you and a god of {hw_foe} side by side. The first of Ondine's islands comes up out of the sea, wet and astonished, with its old village still on it. Ondine stands on the beach with Castor and Tamsin. She has not smiled in the whole of the talks. She does now.

effects.log: Tamsin is mortified and delighted. The island keeps her name, and every other island's name comes back with it.
You keep pulling for a century. It is the longest and best work of your life. The peace holds the whole time.

events.text: A small world called Ammery lies directly under {hw_field}, and its god, a young and very frightened weather-god named Gale, has run away from it to hide in your hall. "Every battle up there is a storm down there," Gale says. "I cannot keep up. I do not know whose side my rain is on."

choices.text: Let Gale stay, and keep Ammery's weather yourself

effects.log: You keep a small world's weather in your evenings, between battles. It is like keeping a garden in a hurricane.

choices.text: Send Gale back with {hw_friend} to help

effects.log: {hw_friend} goes down with Gale and teaches the young god to bend the war's storms out to sea. It mostly works.

events.text: On Ammery, a lighthouse keeper named Marta Quill has noticed. She keeps a log of the sky, and for {hw_years} years it has been full of lights and storms no almanac predicts. She has worked out that something is fighting up there. Her son Benno wants to be a priest of it. Marta prays only one thing, every night: please take it somewhere else.

choices.text: Send Marta a dream that tells her the truth

effects.log: She wakes and writes it in the log, very calmly: there is a war in heaven. Benno reads it and becomes a priest of peace instead.

choices.text: Leave her be, and answer her prayer quietly

effects.log: You do not speak to her. But the storms over her lighthouse grow gentler. Marta notes it in the log as a small mercy.

events.text: The battle is coming to {hw_field} again, the largest of the war, and it will be fought directly over Ammery. Gale is beside you, white as fog. Marta's lighthouse is the only light on that whole coast, and every ship below is steering by it.

choices.text: Shield Ammery with your own body

effects.log: You stand between the battle and the world all day. Nothing reaches Ammery but a little rain. You come home barely standing.

choices.text: Draw the battle off to an empty sky

ok.log: You lure {hw_foe} three skies over, to a place with no worlds under it. Ammery sees only distant lightning.

fail.log: You draw half the battle off. The other half falls on Ammery's sea. Marta's light stays lit, and the ships come in.

events.text: Ammery is whole. Marta Quill is very old now, and she has written in her log that on the worst day of the war something stood between her coast and the sky, and that it looked, she thought, tired. Benno, now a priest, has built a shrine at the foot of the lighthouse with no name on it. Gale wants to know whether you would like your name put on.

effects.log: It stays nameless. Ships below pass it and dip their lights, not knowing to whom. You find you like that best.

choices.text: Let Gale put the name on

effects.log: Your name goes on. A small world prays to you by name for a thousand years. It is a kind of wound and a kind of home.

events.text: The Domain of Lanterns has fallen to {hw_foe}: every lamp lit in a hundred thousand worlds was kept from there. Its old keeper Ivo, a stooped god with soot on his sleeves, has arrived in your camp carrying the one lantern he saved. "They will let them go out," he says. "They do not know which ones matter."

choices.text: Promise Ivo you will take it back

effects.log: You promise. Ivo hangs his lantern on your tent pole, and it burns all through the war.
He tells you, all night: a reading lamp in a cell, a window left lit for a son. You understand what was lost.

events.text: You go in secret to see the Domain of Lanterns. It is not going out. Its new keeper for {hw_foe}, a young goddess named Seraphine, is walking the rows with a long taper, relighting lamps as they gutter. She sees you. She does not raise the alarm. "Ivo left a list," she says. "I am using it."

effects.log: You talk until dawn among the lamps. She loves the domain as much as Ivo does. That is not what you expected to find.

choices.text: Leave before you are seen by anyone else

effects.log: You slip away. You do not tell Ivo that the lamps are well kept. You are not sure why.

events.text: The chance comes: {hw_foe}'s wing at the Domain of Lanterns is pulled away to another front. Only Seraphine and a handful of keepers are left. Ivo is at your shoulder. Your wing could take the domain by morning. Or you could walk in alone, with Ivo, and talk.

ok.log: You take it by morning. Nobody is hurt, and not a lamp goes out. Seraphine is a prisoner, very angry.

fail.log: You take it, but in the fighting a whole row of lamps goes dark. Somewhere below, a hundred windows go black.

choices.text: Walk in with Ivo, and offer to share the keeping

effects.log: You walk in under a lantern instead of a banner. Seraphine and Ivo look at each other for a long time, over the lamps.

events.text: The Domain of Lanterns is yours again, and Seraphine is in your camp as a prisoner of war. Ivo has gone to see her every evening. He comes to you with a request: that she be paroled to the domain, under him, to keep the rows he cannot reach any more. "She knows the list," he says. "She learned it better than I did."

effects.log: Seraphine keeps the far rows under Ivo until the war ends, and after. When Ivo fades, the lanterns are hers, and none go out.

choices.text: Refuse, and send her home in the exchange

effects.log: She goes home. Ivo keeps the domain alone, slowly. A few far lamps go out every year, and he names each one.

effects.log: You walk in under a lantern instead of a banner. Seraphine and Ivo look at each other for a long time, over the lamps.

events.text: The Domain of Lanterns is yours again, and Seraphine is in your camp as a prisoner of war. Ivo has gone to see her every evening. He comes to you with a request: that she be paroled to the domain, under him, to keep the rows he cannot reach any more. "She knows the list," he says. "She learned it better than I did."

effects.log: Seraphine keeps the far rows under Ivo until the war ends, and after. When Ivo fades, the lanterns are hers, and none go out.

choices.text: Refuse, and send her home in the exchange

effects.log: She goes home. Ivo keeps the domain alone, slowly. A few far lamps go out every year, and he names each one.

events.text: The Domain of Lanterns is kept by two now: Ivo for your side, Seraphine for {hw_foe}, under a truce nobody above you signed. The war goes on all round it. In the middle of it, a hundred thousand worlds keep their lamps lit. Your side's high command has found out, and wants to know what exactly you think you are doing.

effects.log: You tell them about the reading lamp and the window left lit. They are not moved. But after the war the shared keeping is written into the peace, word for word.

choices.text: Argue that a lit domain is a held domain

ok.log: They accept it, grudgingly. The lamps stay lit, and both keepers stay.

fail.log: They do not accept it. You are reprimanded. The lamps stay lit anyway, because Ivo and Seraphine do not ask permission.
